Temperature exerts competing influence on sorption, transport, deformation, and energy redistribution, while TDC combines high gas-storage capacity, low permeability, and low mechanical strength, favoring pressure disequilibrium and structural instability. Three priority research questions emerge: quantifying adsorbed-gas energy conversion into dynamic work, establishing cross-scale similarity and validation for thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) coupling, and developing physics-constrained prediction of nonlinear instability. These advances provide a pathway from single-index hazard identification toward mechanism-informed, multiparameter early warning.

item.title: Site-Selective Oxidative Degradation of the Conserved Disulfide Bridge in Oxytocin and Vasopressin: Chemical Transformations and Structural Destabilization
item.description:
Abstract
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are major mediators of oxidative stress and represent an important source of chemical instability for biologically relevant molecules, including disulfide-containing peptides. Oxytocin and vasopressin are important signaling neuropeptides whose biological activity critically depends on the structural integrity of a conserved Cys1–Cys6 disulfide bridge. Here, we investigated the oxidative degradation pathways of both peptides under controlled ROS-generating conditions using UV–C irradiation as a reproducible source of radical stress. Structural and chemical changes were monitored by circular dichroism spectroscopy and HPLC–mass spectrometry. Both peptides underwent progressive degradation with prominent modifications of the disulfide bridge, which emerged as a major site of radical attack. Oxidative degradation produced thioether and polysulfide-containing species consistent with disulfide-bridge modification involving cysteine desulfurization and rearrangement, while CD spectroscopy revealed early loss of the disulfide-constrained cyclic structure before extensive degradation occurred. Control experiments employing thiol- and disulfide-reactive reagents further supported the key role of the disulfide bridge in determining peptide susceptibility to oxidative damage. Removal or modification of the sulfur-containing residues significantly altered degradation kinetics and product distribution. These results identify the conserved Cys1–Cys6 disulfide bridge as a major target of ROS-induced degradation in oxytocin and vasopressin under oxidative conditions and provide new insight into the chemical pathways associated with oxidative modification of cyclic disulfide-containing peptides. More broadly, these findings establish a framework for future investigations into whether redox chemistry and oxidative stress contribute to the regulation or dysregulation of oxytocin and vasopressin stability and signaling.

item.title: Heteroaryl-Substituted Secondary Amines as Multifunctional Antimicrobial, Antibiofilm, Acetylcholinesterase, and α-Glucosidase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
A series of heteroaryl-substituted secondary amine derivatives (6a–g and 7a–g) were synthesized by reduction of Schiff bases obtained in our previous study with sodium borohydride (NaBH4). The molecules were characterized by spectroscopic techniques including 1H NMR, 13C NMR, FTIR, and GC-MS. Following synthesis, all compounds underwent extensive biological investigation, including studies of their antimicrobial, antifungal, antibiofilm, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities, as well as their effects on membrane integrity and molecular docking capabilities. Some molecules exhibited measurable antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida tropicalis. Among the tested derivatives, compound 6a exhibited the lowest MIC90 values against E. coli (749.1 μg/mL) and C. tropicalis (840.2 μg/mL), whereas compound 7d showed the lowest MIC90 value against S. aureus (789.1 μg/mL). In antibiofilm tests, compound 7e maintained high inhibitory activity even at low concentrations, while compound 7b showed the highest single-point biofilm inhibition. Membrane integrity studies revealed significant DNA and protein leakage effects, particularly for compounds 7c and 7g. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) analysis revealed compound-dependent differences in oxidative stress generation, suggesting that ROS production may contribute to the observed antimicrobial effects. In enzyme inhibition studies, compounds 6d and 6f emerged as the strongest AChE inhibitors with IC50 values of 89.17 and 73.35 μM, respectively, while compound 7a showed the strongest α-glucosidase inhibitory activity (IC50 = 173.92 μM). Molecular docking studies provided plausible binding modes and predicted interactions of the selected active compounds within the investigated target proteins.

item.title: Vanadyl Sulfate Embedded in Poly(ethylene glycol) for the Selective Aerobic Aromatic Alcohol Oxidation to Carbonyl Compounds
item.description:
Abstract
A poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based composite containing a well-defined, molecular neutral vanadyl sulfate compound was synthesized in dimethylacetamide (DMA) and characterized. The composite material catalyzed the aerobic oxidation of selected aromatic alcohols to carbonyl compounds in DMA (homogeneous reaction condition) under high selectivity, using a very low amount of vanadium (0.5 mol %). The catalytic activity of the composite material turned out to be significantly superior to that of the bare vanadium compound and to reported catalytic results stemming from vanadyl-based catalyst, which use either high reaction temperature and vanadium loading or toxic and expensive additives (i.e. a TOF value for benzyl alcohol conversion of 57 h–1). PEG turned out to be important not only for the catalytic activity of the vanadium-based catalyst but also for the efficient recovery of vanadium. The deactivation of the molecular vanadium catalyst studied by independent recycling experiments and spectroscopic analyses carried out on the recovered catalyst turned out to be due to the formation of polymeric V(III)-O-V(III) species.

item.title: Sequential Electrochemical Construction of Hierarchical LIG/PPy/MnO 2 Microsupercapacitors with High Areal Capacitance and Device-Level Stability
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving high areal energy storage in flexible microsupercapacitors while maintaining compatibility with direct planar patterning remains challenging, particularly when multiple pseudocapacitive components must be sequentially integrated without compromising electrode accessibility or device level performance. In this paper, we develop a sequential electrochemical construction strategy to integrate polypyrrole (PPy) and manganese dioxide (MnO2) directly onto interdigitated laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes without preformed composite powders, slurry casting, or polymer binders. Porous LIG serves as the conductive framework and current collector, followed by in situ PPy electropolymerization and subsequent MnO2 electrodeposition. Systematic control of LIG processing, PPy growth, MnO2 deposition, and gel electrolyte composition establishes a fabrication window that balances electrical conductivity, pseudocapacitive material loading, and structural accessibility while preserving the underlying porous LIG architecture. Stepwise LIG, LIG/PPy, and LIG/PPy/MnO2 controls exhibit the same performance hierarchy at both the individual electrode and complete device levels, demonstrating that the electrochemical gains introduced during sequential functionalization are retained after complete microsupercapacitor (MSC) assembly. The resulting LIG/PPy/MnO2 device delivers an areal capacitance of 621.2 mF cm–2 at 0.37 mA cm–2 and a maximum areal energy density of 55.22 μWh cm–2 at 0.1494 mW cm–2. Extended rate measurements further demonstrate continued electrochemical operation up to 5 mA cm–2 under substantially increased current demand. The device retains 97.04% of its flat state capacitance at 180° static bending, exhibits a device-to-device RSD of 2.29%, retains 94.5% capacitance after 60 days of ambient storage, and maintains 85.1% after 5000 GCD cycles. Series integration further extends the operating voltage from 0.8 to 2.4 V with predictable electrical scaling and enables three MSCs to power a red LED for approximately 183 s. These results establish a directly patterned and independently controlled approach for translating hierarchical pseudocapacitive construction into high areal energy storage, reproducible device performance, and scalable voltage output.

item.title: A Dermal-Epidermal Junction-Inclusive Skin Model Enabled by Controllable Hydrogel Swelling
item.description:
Abstract
Tissue engineered skin models are important tools for the in vitro study of physiological and pathophysiological processes as well as the evaluation of therapeutic strategies and the efficacy of pharmaceutical and cosmetic compounds. Replicating the functional anatomy of cutaneous tissue is a crucial aspect in ensuring that observations made using these models are translatable to the actual situation in native skin. However, most contemporary full-thickness skin models neglect the reconstruction of the undulated microtopography of the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ), which not only contributes to the biological functionality of the skin (e.g., stem cell niches), but also affects tissue mechanics and drug diffusion. Herein, we fabricated bilayer skin models with DEJ-like microtopographies introduced by interfacial wrinkling between a hydrogel and a nanofibrous membrane through a controllable swelling–deswelling approach. The interfacial wrinkles contributed to the structural integrity of the bilayer models. Their formation could be induced in the presence of living cells through mechanical stress-driven buckling instabilities, thus differentiating the process from commonly used prepatterning techniques. The bilayer models supported the coculture of human dermal fibroblasts and human epidermal keratinocytes and the formation of stratified epithelia. Our findings provide a potential alternative method to introduce DEJ-like anatomical features into full-thickness skin tissue models.

item.title: Valorization of Cannabis sativa Residual Biomass from Industrial CBD Extraction as a Renewable Support for Candida antarctica Lipase B Immobilization and Fatty Acid Esterification
item.description:
Abstract
Residual Cannabis sativa biomass from industrial CBD extraction in ethanol was evaluated as a renewable support for the immobilization of Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) by physical adsorption, and the resulting biocatalysts were applied to the esterification of long-chain fatty acids with ethanol. Because extractives released by the untreated biomass interfered with protein quantification, three simple pretreatments were compared. Milling alone, with or without buffer washing, gave reproducible immobilization and active, reusable biocatalysts, whereas SDS washing increased protein retention but led to nearly inactive preparations, indicating that protein loading alone does not predict catalytic performance. The milling-only biocatalyst converted two industrial palm fatty acid distillate fractions with conversions comparable to those of Novozym 435, retained more than 80% of its initial conversion after five cycles, and was operated in a continuous-flow packed-bed reactor with conversions of 95% or higher at a residence time of 15 min. These results indicate that this residue is a low-cost, minimally processed support for lipase-catalyzed esterification.

item.title: Valorization of Cellulose Sludge as a Sodium Alginate-Based Bioadsorbent for Bromazepam Removal from Water
item.description:
Abstract
The remediation of benzodiazepine residues from industrial discharge remains a critical environmental challenge due to their chemical stability and neurotoxic potential. In this study, cellulose sludge from the pulp-and-paper industry was successfully upcycled into Ca2+-cross-linked sodium alginate hydrogel beads for the targeted removal of bromazepam (BZP). This work represents the first systematic investigation into BZP sequestration using a waste-derived hybrid hydrogel, at deliberately low concentrations (0.5–5.4 mg L–1), kept as close to environmentally relevant levels as the analytical method allows and within the range reported for point-source pharmaceutical effluents. The beads exhibited a rough filamentous surface and an interconnected 3D porous network characterized by a mesoporous texture (SSA: 9.35 m2 g–1; pore volume: 0.04 cm3 g–1) and an amphoteric surface (pHPZC = 8.04). Kinetic studies revealed a rapid initial uptake reaching an experimental capacity of 0.25 mg g–1 at 180 min, with the Elovich model providing the best statistical fit (R2 = 0.994; AIC = −56.9; BIC = −56.7), consistent with adsorption on energetically heterogeneous sites governed by coverage-dependent rate decay. Because the isotherms were measured in this dilute range, no saturation plateau was reached: the equilibrium data were best described by the Freundlich model at 25 °C and by a linear (Henry-type) model at 35 and 45 °C. The hydrogel beads were efficiently regenerated using 0.1 M HCl, maintaining structural integrity and performance across four consecutive cycles (BZP removal of approximately 13–15% in each cycle, with no systematic decline). This study provides a sustainable, zero-waste strategy for the valorization of abundant industrial residues into functional bioadsorbents, directly supporting circular economy goals for emerging contaminant mitigation.

item.title: Compatibility and Insecticidal Responses of Bacillus thuringiensis in Tank Mixtures with Spray Adjuvants against Spodoptera frugiperda
item.description:
Abstract
The fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, is a major agricultural pest whose management increasingly relies on Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)-based bioinsecticides. However, tank-mix applications with adjuvants may alter Bt performance. This study evaluated the in vitro compatibility of Bt (Xentari) combined with five commercial adjuvants (Li-700, Fighter, Wetcit Gold, Protac, and Tween 80) and compared the insecticidal responses of these mixtures in laboratory bioassays. In vitro compatibility was assessed using nutrient agar to determine vegetative growth and sporulation, while pH variation was measured in laboratory spray solutions over time. Insecticidal response was evaluated through bioassays on artificial diet with second-instar S. frugiperda, using two complementary approaches: spore suspensions derived from in vitro assays and laboratory assays with spray solutions applied at 0, 2, 6, and 24 h after preparation. Tween 80 increased vegetative growth, whereas Li-700 reduced vegetative growth but enhanced sporulation. Wetcit Gold and Protac completely inhibited Bt development in vitro. Protac reduced solution pH below 2.5, indicating strongly acidic conditions. Under the laboratory conditions evaluated, microbiological compatibility observed in vitro did not consistently correspond directly to the insecticidal responses obtained in the artificial-diet bioassays. All Bt-containing spray solutions resulted in final mortality above 80%. Within the Wetcit Gold treatment, final mortality at 2 h was lower than at 6 and 24 h, while no significant differences among Bt-containing treatments were detected within individual resting times. These findings indicate that microbiological compatibility assays and laboratory bioassays provide complementary information for interpreting Bt–adjuvant interactions.

item.title: Flexible Receptor Docking Provides Structural Models for the Recognition of 2-Amino-heteroaryl-benzothiazole-6-anilide Derivatives by Lck via the CorrEA Method
item.description:
Abstract
Structural models of Lck bound to a chemically diverse series of 62 2-amino-heteroaryl-benzothiazole-6-anilide (AHBA) inhibitors were built to examine how the conformational state of the ATP-binding site shapes the structure-based interpretation of their potency. Docking to the static Lck crystal structure (PDB entry 1QPC) generated plausible complexes for only 54 of the 62 compounds, and produced essentially no relationship between docking scores and experimental pIC50 values, indicating that a single receptor conformation cannot capture how this scaffold is recognized. Receptor flexibility was then introduced through the CorrEA protocol, which cross-docks the series against an ensemble of Lck conformations sampled by molecular dynamics (MD) and, using the measured activities of the series as a reference, selects for each ligand the receptor–pose pair that best accounts for the observed potencies. The resulting ensemble accommodated the entire compound set, overcoming the inability of the rigid receptor to host eight of the derivatives, while preserving the canonical orientation of the AHBA scaffold within the ATP-binding site. The ensemble also recovered the hinge and gatekeeper hydrogen bonds to M319 and T316 expected for ATP-competitive protein kinase (PK) inhibitors, which were only partially satisfied in the rigid-receptor poses. Examination of the selected conformations indicates that the series is accommodated through modest, coordinated rearrangements distributed across the glycine-rich loop, the region beyond the hinge, and the back pocket, rather than through a single dominant conformational change. These models offer an activity-consistent structural framework for interpreting ligand recognition by Lck and a transferable workflow for PKs whose binding sites are conformationally labile.

item.title: Connecting Conformational Landscapes with Bioactivity in Macrocyclic Kinase Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Macrocyclization can improve the selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties of kinase inhibitors, yet the conformational basis of these effects remains incompletely understood. Here, we characterized the structures and conformational ensembles of the clinically relevant macrocyclic kinase inhibitors pacritinib and zotiraciclib using microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED), NMR spectroscopy, and molecular docking. Both compounds populate a set of related macrocyclic core conformations, with additional conformational adaptability arising from changes in aromatic torsion angles and substituent orientations. These conformational adaptations correlate with physicochemical properties relevant to aqueous solubility and membrane permeability. Pacritinib exhibits chameleonic behavior through environment-dependent modulation of its exposed polar surface area, whereas protonation of zotiraciclib generates distinct conformational states stabilized by intramolecular cation–π interactions. Molecular docking indicates that the experimentally determined conformations are compatible with productive binding across multiple kinase targets. Collectively, these findings establish a link between conformational adaptability, physicochemical properties, and polypharmacology in macrocyclic kinase inhibitors, providing insights that may guide the rational design of future macrocyclic therapeutics.

item.title: Fluoride-Free Siloxane Circularity at Room Temperature: Tetrabutylammonium Hydroxide as a Dual-Functional De- and Repolymerization Initiator for Silicone Oils, Elastomers, and Hybrid Coatings
item.description:
Abstract
With increasing EU restrictions on fluoride chemistries and their toxicity related to the potential generation of hydrofluoric acid (HF) as well as their corrosivity, there is an urgent need to develop fluoride-free depolymerization methods to enable safe and sustainable siloxane recycling. In this regard, we here present a fluoride-free, at room-temperature (RT) operating depolymerization method, where tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH), identified as a highly effective dual-functional de- and repolymerization initiator, transforms silicone-based elastomers into reusable cyclic siloxanes. Thereby, the solvent/polymer ratio (v/w) is the key for controlling the product distribution: at 10/1 (v/w), the depolymerization mixture shifts from D4-rich to high proportions of byproducts greater than 40 mol % and ultimately stops the process, leaving solid educt silicone at even lower dilutions. Under optimized reaction conditions above a threshold of 0.29/1 (w/w) for the TBAOH/polymer ratio, a relative proportion of up to 88 mol % cyclic siloxanes (D3 to D5), with D4 as the main product, is obtained. This corresponds to 77 mol % absolute NMR conversion into cyclic siloxanes. Additionally, it is worth noting that the fluoride-free, RT operating reaction conditions are effective for a very broad educt scope ranging from linear polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) oils, (filled) Pt-cross-linked silicone elastomers, to inorganic–organic hybrid polymers and coatings. Compared to sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as an alkaline reference, TBAOH affords fewer noncyclic byproducts (12–26 mol % vs 25–30 mol %) and a higher D3 (4–14 mol % vs 1–3 mol %) relative proportion, highlighting its distinct reactivity. Fluoride-free siloxane circularity is demonstrated at RT by two complementary repolymerization routes. Within the first method, TBAOH uniquely acts as the initiator for both the depolymerization and the subsequent anionic ring-opening polymerization (AROP) without prior workup, while the second involves the isolation of cyclic siloxanes followed by base-catalyzed AROP. Thus, this TBAOH-enabled, fluoride-free depolymerization method, which operates at RT, provides tunable product distributions and a broad substrate applicability for practical silicone circularity.

item.title: Moringa oleifera Alginate-Based Beads for Adsorption of Selected Heavy Metals: Preparation, Kinetics, Isotherms, and Reusability Studies
item.description:
Abstract
Moringa oleifera (MO) leaf powder, a low-cost natural resource, has been extensively used for the removal of heavy metals from water. To overcome challenges associated with powdered adsorbents, including difficult separation and low recovery, this study details the synthesis and evaluation of MO-alginate (MO-Alg) bead adsorbents for the adsorption of arsenic, cadmium, iron, chromium, zinc, and lead from oil-polluted aqueous samples. The beads were prepared through ionic gelation using sodium alginate (SA) as an encapsulation matrix with varying MO loadings. SEM analysis revealed that MO-Alg beads were spherical with a rough and cracked surface texture compared to smooth pristine sodium alginate (SA) beads, while XRD analysis confirmed the amorphous nature of both materials. At pH 5, MO (4 g) beads achieved the highest adsorption efficiencies. Kinetic studies followed the pseudo-second-order model, while equilibrium data fitted the Langmuir model for As(III) and Cr(VI) and the Freundlich isotherm model for Cd(II), Pb(II), Zn(II), and Fe(III). The Langmuir isotherm model estimated maximum adsorption capacities of 44.22, 61.11, 41.16, 59.14, 55.22, and 76.69 mg/g for As(III), Cd(II), Cr(VI), Fe(III), Pb(II), and Zn(II), respectively, at 25 °C. Negative ΔG° and positive ΔH° values over 25–45 °C confirmed that the adsorption process was spontaneous and endothermic. Reusability tests demonstrated that MO-Alg (1:1) beads maintained strong adsorption performance after seven regeneration cycles with removal efficiencies above 70% for Pb(II), Cd(II), and Zn(II), while As(III), Cr(VI), and Fe(III) remained effective up to six cycles with efficiencies above 60%. Overall, MO-Alg beads have great potential as an inexpensive sorbent for the removal of toxic heavy metals.

item.title: Carbon Nanofiber-Integrated CuCo-MOF as a Conductive Bifunctional Electrocatalyst for Overall Water Splitting
item.description:
Abstract
The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst, with a well-defined microstructure and efficient charge transfer was successfully synthesized through a simple solvothermal method. In the CuCo-MOF/CNF composite, the introduction of CNF can effectively improve the conductivity and provide sufficient active sites for the electrochemical reaction. The CuCo-MOF/CNF composite has excellent bifunctional electrocatalytic activity for the HER and OER reactions. The catalyst really stands out with its great performance, requiring overpotentials of 50 mV for HER and 70 mV for OER at a current density of 10 mA cm–2. The CuCo-MOF/CNF electrocatalyst has low Tafel slope values of 98 mV dec–1 for OER and 131 mV dec–1 for HER, along with low charge transfer resistance, exhibiting excellent operational stability for up to 40 h for both OER and HER. Moreover, the catalyst has relatively large double-layer capacitance values of 8.95 mF cm–2 for OER and 3.47 mF cm–2 for HER, implying that the electrochemically active surface areas are quite large (223.8 cm2 for OER and 86.8 cm2 for HER). Overall, these structural and electrochemical advantages contribute to the superior catalytic performance of the electrocatalyst, providing a novel framework for the development of highly efficient and scalable bifunctional electrocatalysts for overall water splitting.

item.title: Effects of Tiger Tail Sea Cucumber Bohadschia argus on Wound Healing In Vitro and In Vivo Using an Acute Rat Model Infected with Staphylococcus aureus
item.description:
Abstract
Infectious wounds caused by Staphylococcus aureus remain a significant clinical challenge due to delayed healing and increasing antimicrobial resistance, necessitating alternative therapeutic strategies. This study aimed to evaluate the wound-healing potential of the ethanol extract of the tiger tail sea cucumber Bohadschia argus (EEBA) through integrated in vitro, in vivo, and in silico approaches. Phytochemical profiling using LC-HRMS identified 260 metabolites, and 12 prioritized compounds were selected for molecular docking analysis. EEBA demonstrated concentration-dependent antioxidant activity in the nitric oxide scavenging assay and inhibitory effects on protein denaturation, indicating anti-inflammatory potential, although differences compared to controls were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). In an excisional wound model in Staphylococcus aureus-infected Wistar rats, topical application of 1% EEBA accelerated wound contraction and improved macroscopic healing compared to the negative control. Histopathological evaluation revealed reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, enhanced fibroblast proliferation, increased angiogenesis, and improved collagen organization across the inflammatory, proliferative, and maturation phases. Hemolysis testing confirmed good biocompatibility with negligible erythrocyte lysis (<5%). Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding affinities of selected compounds toward key inflammatory targets, including TNF-α, NF-κB, and FLAP, as well as antibacterial targets relevant to Staphylococcus aureus, namely, DNA gyrase-B, dihydrofolate reductase, and penicillin-binding protein. These findings provide preliminary mechanistic insights into the potential wound-healing and antibacterial activities of EEBA. Overall, EEBA exhibits promising wound-healing activity in an infected wound model through modulation of oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways, with selected metabolites also showing potential interactions with bacterial targets associated with S. aureus infection. These findings support the potential development of EEBA as a natural therapeutic candidate for infected wound management.

item.title: Investigating Ferritin Permeability to Metal-Based Drugs through Molecular Dynamics
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, we implemented a workflow based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to assess whether gold(I)-containing complexes can traverse the C3 channels of human H ferritin and which energetic barriers were at play in the process. By using two example complexes for which an extensive experimental characterization was already available, we observed that classical MD correctly indicated which one could spontaneously pass through the channel. To quantify the ability of the ferritin nanocage to retain the internalized complex, we estimated, through steered MD and umbrella sampling simulations, the Potential of Mean Force (PMF) along the pathway from the interior to the exterior. The results reveal a steep energetic barrier that hinders the exit of the complex once internalized. In contrast, the second complex encounters steric and electrostatic repulsion, which prevents its internalization. Analysis of protein-complex contacts shows that the successful translocation of the first complex is electrostatically guided through a sequence of transient interactions with Asp/Glu residues lining the pore. The comparison of these two complexes demonstrates that the C3 channel of ferritin only attracts positively charged species and that the nanocage creates a strongly asymmetric energy landscape for charged complexes. This provides a mechanistic explanation for experimental observations of loading in ferritin. Overall, the work demonstrates a computational approach for assessing the permeability of metal-based drugs through ferritin channels and offers molecular insight into channel-mediated transport processes.

item.title: Fractionation and Identification of Bioactive Peptides from Camel Skin Hydrolysate: In Silico and Molecular Docking Analysis
item.description:
Abstract
Hypertension and glycemia disorders are severe issues in public health, highlighting the urgent need for the discovery of natural bioactive agents with health benefits. In this sense, the present study examines camel skin gelatin hydrolyzate, obtained using Alcalase (GHA). GHA was first ultrafiltrated, and the low molecular weight fraction (<10 kDa) with the highest in vitro ACE and DPP-IV inhibitory activities (82.75% and 72.5%, respectively) was further purified by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography. Among the resulting fractions (FI to FV), FIII and FIV were the most potent inhibitors against the ACE activity. Thus, they were analyzed by LC-MS/MS for peptide identification. In silico and peptidomic analyses revealed several novel peptide sequences. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA studies were subsequently performed to investigate the interactions and estimate the binding energies of the selected peptides with ACE and DPP-IV. Among the investigated peptides, GPSGPSGL and GPSGPR showed the strongest energy-binding scores against the studied enzymes with favorable interactions with their active sites. In conclusion, hydrolyzed camel skin gelatin is a promising source of multifunctional bioactive peptides and a potential natural ingredient for the management of hypertension and glycemic disorders.

item.title: Biocatalytic Valorization of Used Soybean Cooking Oil for Furfuryl Esters Production: Effects of Alcohol Feeding Strategy and Water Removal on Immobilized Lipase Performance and Stability
item.description:
Abstract
This study describes an efficient biocatalytic process for the synthesis of furfuryl esters from used soybean cooking oil (USCO). The process involves the hydrolysis of USCO using free Candida rugosa lipase, followed by solvent-free esterification of the resulting free fatty acids (FFAs) with furfuryl alcohol (FA) catalyzed by immobilized lipase Eversa Transform 2.0 (ET2.0). Five supports, including acid-treated rice husks with fine (FRH) and coarse (CRH) particle sizes, commercial and rice husk-derived octyl-functionalized silica, and poly(styrene-divinylbenzene) (PSty-DVB), were evaluated for ET2.0 immobilization by physical adsorption. Among the evaluated supports, PSty-DVB provided the highest immobilized protein loading (31.3 ± 1.1 mg g–1) and the best overall catalytic performance in furfuryl esters synthesis. Using this biocatalyst, FFAs conversion reached approximately 94% within 60 min at 45 °C under solvent-free conditions and with a slight excess of FA (FFAs:FA molar ratio of 1:1.15). The combination of stepwise furfuryl alcohol feeding and molecular sieves for in situ water removal improved biocatalyst operational stability, allowing the retention of approximately 95% of the initial activity after 15 consecutive esterification cycles. These results show that ET2.0 immobilized on PSty-DVB is a suitable biocatalyst for the solvent-free conversion of waste-derived fatty acids into furfuryl esters.

item.title: Polyelectrolyte Nature of Model Colloidal Plastics and Their Impact on Molecular Adsorption
item.description:
Abstract
Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are pervasive environmental pollutants, yet their interfacial structures and molecular adsorption behaviors remain poorly understood. This study investigates the polyelectrolyte nature of model colloidal micro- and nanoplastics (CMNPs)─specifically polystyrene particles featuring plain, sulfate, or carboxylate surface functional groups─and examines how these features dictate molecular adsorption and electrokinetic properties. Using a combination of in situ dynamic light scattering (DLS), electrophoretic mobility measurements, surface-selective second harmonic generation (SHG) spectroscopy, and by relying on previous theoretical and experimental work, we demonstrate that CMNPs possess a soft, hydrated, polyelectrolyte-rich interfacial layer. This brush-like or “hairy” architecture persists regardless of the specific surface functional group and fundamentally alters particle behavior in aqueous media. Electrokinetic measurements reveal nonclassical trends in electrophoretic mobility under increasing electrolyte concentrations, matching theoretical frameworks for soft colloids while contradicting classical hard sphere models. Furthermore, SHG adsorption isotherms for a model cationic dye (DASPI) show that adsorption affinity is governed by a combination of electrostatic and entropic effects, with hydrogen bonding serving as a strong possibility for carboxylated particles. Notably, the adsorption affinity is less sensitive to electrolyte concentration than predicted by classical models, indicating that volumetric charge density and interfacial hydration are likely the primary determinants governing organic molecule adsorption at the CMNP/aqueous interface. By overturning the conventional view of microplastics as rigid, inert particles, these findings highlight the critical importance of accounting for soft, hydrated interfaces when predicting the transport, environmental fate, and contaminant interactions of plastic pollution in natural waters.

item.title: The Effect of Design Parameters on Yields of 33 Harmful and Potentially Harmful Constituents (HPHCs) in Mainstream Smoke of Large Cigars
item.description:
Abstract
The effect of large cigar (LC) design parameters on the mainstream smoke yields of harmful and potentially harmful constituents (HPHCs) is relatively unstudied. Available chemical analysis research on LCs has focused on tar and a limited number of HPHCs (e.g., nicotine, carbon monoxide, benzo[a]pyrene, acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, and acrolein), while many smoke HPHCs have been largely overlooked. Recently, Cheng et al. reported the smoke yields of 33 less commonly studied HPHCs in 10 LC brands generated by the Canadian Intense smoking regimen (55 mL puff volume, 30 s puff frequency, 2 s puff duration, 100% vent block, if applicable). In this study, we compared their previously reported HPHC yields to cigar design parameters (weight, length, circumference, pressure drop, and calculated density and volume) using simple linear regression to determine if any correlations exist that may support future in-depth study. The impact of each design parameter on individual HPHC yields was evaluated using the slopes and correlation coefficients (r2) of the linear regression lines, with P values indicating the significance of the slope. Cigar weight and calculated volume were positively associated with the yields of tobacco alkaloids (anabasine, nornicotine), carbonyls (acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, propionaldehyde), and some volatile and semivolatile (VSV) organic compounds (ethylbenzene, styrene, 2,3-benzofuran, furan), while also being negatively associated with polyaromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) yields. Cigar length was also positively associated with tobacco alkaloids, carbonyls, and VSVs, but did not influence PAH yields. Like weight and volume, higher cigar circumference was associated with lower PAH and heterocyclic aromatic amine yields, but it only had a weaker positive association with tobacco alkaloids, carbonyls, and VSVs. Calculated density and pressure drop were not associated with any consistent or meaningful differences in HPHC yields. These preliminary and rudimentary results suggest that simple design parameters influence HPHC yields in large cigars in a predictable manner. Having a better understanding of how parameters influence HPHC yields can inform evaluations of the public health impact of large cigars and public communications about their health risks.

item.title: Polymer Solution Entanglement Influences the Mechanical Properties of the Resultant Electrospun Fibers
item.description:
Abstract
Electrospun fibers have a range of applications that rely on specific mechanical properties for optimal function. In this study, we examined the diameter-independent relationship between polymer solution entanglement and the mechanical properties of individual electrospun polycaprolactone fibers. Molecular weights of 35 kDa, 45 kDa, and 80 kDa were used at various concentrations to produce smooth fibers from polymer solutions across a range of entanglement molecular weights. Fibers were pulled until failure using atomic force microscopy, and their mechanical properties were determined. Because of the strong diameter dependence, we selected fibers within a limited range to compare initial modulus, rupture stress, and toughness. Within the same polymer molecular weight, the initial modulus, extensibility, rupture stress, and toughness increased with greater polymer solution entanglement. However, when comparing across polymer molecular weights, we observed that changing molecular weight altered extensibility to a greater degree than adjusting entanglement. The fibers produced from 35 kDa PCL had significantly smaller diameters, around 100 nm, than those produced at higher molecular weights, and their mechanical properties did not change with entanglement. These results suggest that fiber mechanics can be controlled and tailored to specific applications through diameter-independent means by altering entanglement and polymer molecular weight.

item.title: A pH-Responsive Fine Powder Coating Strategy for Simultaneous Taste Masking and Physical Modification of Herbal Extract
item.description:
Abstract
Herbal extracts are widely used as intermediates and fundamental materials in pharmaceutical processing. However, the pronounced drawback in powder flowability and intensely bitter taste present major obstacles to the innovation of herbal-derived oral dosage forms. Here, we report a fine powder coating strategy to overcome these challenges for an internally developed herbal extract that exhibits these drawbacks. By employing a tangential fluidized-bed coater, a composite polymer coating formulation was applied to the extract powder. Such a coating formulation achieved rapid release performance under acidic condition and sustained release performance under neutral condition, confirmed by dissolution and kinetic studies. The effect of coating modification on the extract powder was characterized by powder flowability measurements, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analyses. We further demonstrated the efficacy of the taste masking strategy using an electronic tongue system. Our work provides a practical and feasible paradigm for coating fine herbal extract powders, presenting new perspectives for the development of modern oral dosage forms designed for pharmaceutical powders suffering from similar challenges.

item.title: FTIR-Based Quantification of a Corrosion Inhibitor in Solution: Experimental Investigation and Quantum-Chemical Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Residual corrosion inhibitor (RCI) monitoring is essential for ensuring the effectiveness of corrosion mitigation programs in oil and gas production systems. Among the available analytical techniques, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) offers advantages such as rapid analysis, minimal sample preparation, and the absence of chemical reagents. In this study, an FTIR-based method was developed for the quantification of 2-phenyl-2-imidazoline (IMDZ), a corrosion inhibitor, and the influence of typical produced-water constituents on its spectroscopic response was investigated. Calibration curves were constructed using IMDZ concentrations ranging from 100 to 1000 ppm in Milli-Q water. Two characteristic spectral regions were evaluated, centered at approximately 1500 and 784 cm–1. The band at 1500 cm–1 exhibited a linear response with concentration (R2 = 0.9922), while the band at 784 cm–1 showed a logarithmic response. The estimated limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) for the 1500 cm–1 band based on within-pellet repeatability were approximately 32 and 96 ppm, respectively. The effects of acetic acid, NaCl, CaCl2, FeCl2, NaHCO3, and dissolved CO2 were evaluated individually at a fixed IMDZ concentration of 500 ppm. Significant matrix effects were observed, particularly in the low-frequency spectral region. Acetic acid and FeCl2 produced the largest spectral perturbations, whereas NaCl caused substantial reductions in peak area. Overall, the 1500 cm–1 band exhibited greater resistance to interference than the 784 cm–1 band. Quantum-chemical calculations revealed strong hydrogen-bond formation between IMDZ and acetic acid, as well as cation−π interactions involving dissolved metal cations. The combined experimental and computational results demonstrate that the spectral region centered at approximately 1500 cm–1 is the most suitable analytical marker for FTIR-based quantification of IMDZ in brine environments.

item.title: Construction of a Dual-Response Fluorescent Probe for Potential Detection of Sulfites and NAD(P)H
item.description:
Abstract
Sulfites, which serve as significant multifunctional food additives, can act as potential pollutants or toxins in vivo when present in excess and can be reduced in association with NAD(P)H. While NAD(P)H is a central redox coenzyme that fuels mitochondrial ATP production, sustains cellular redox balance, and regulates diverse signaling pathways, it would be invaluable to monitor the rapid subcellular fluctuations of NAD(P)H and sulfites for a comprehensive understanding of metabolic syndromes, neurodegenerative disorders, and ischemia-related injuries by constructing a dual-response fluorescent probe. Herein, FL-D was designed and synthesized as an excitation-gated dual-response fluorescent probe that decouples the optical detection of sulfites from cellular reducing power within a single molecular scaffold. Built on a functionalized quinolinium platform, FL-D exhibited spectroscopically orthogonal response modes governed by the excitation wavelength. Under 378 nm excitation, FL-D functioned as a ratiometric sensor for bisulfite and sulfite (HSO3–/SO32–), utilizing intrinsic emission bands at 434 and 510 nm to display a pronounced ratiometric shift with high selectivity against competing biothiols. In contrast, under 500 nm excitation, FL-D entirely bypassed the sulfur-responsive spectral window, operating as a specific turn-on fluorescent reporter for NADH and generating a strong emission enhancement at 577 nm under physiological conditions (up to 100-fold variation), which could potentially monitor fluctuations in NADH and sulfites. Such profound excitation-gated orthogonality should enable independent yet simultaneous interrogation of sulfur metabolism and nicotinamide redox status without reliance on probe cocktails or complex spectral unmixing for further investigation.

item.title: Effect of Guanidine Carbonate on the Optical Properties of KClO 3 –Lactose-Based Orange Smoke-Generating Composition
item.description:
Abstract
To investigate the influence of the nitrogen-rich additive guanidine carbonate (GC) on the optical performance of orange-colored smoke compositions, pyrotechnic formulations with varying GC contents were evaluated using a self-made sealed smoke chamber. A stroboscopic spectrum analyzer and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) were employed to characterize the optical properties of smoke aerosol and compositions of combustion residue and thus elucidate the mechanism by which GC modulates the optical performance of KClO3–lactose-based orange-colored smoke compositions. The results showed that at GC contents of 0–4 wt %, the aerosol exhibited low broadband transmittance, with ΔT suppressed to approximately 1.45%. At a GC content of 8–12 wt %, the early endothermic decomposition and gas evolution of GC eliminate the high-temperature exothermic stage of the system and shorten the time the dye resides in the high-temperature region, which is hypothesized to minimize the thermal degradation of the dye during vaporization. Consequently, ΔT increased sharply to 8.06–8.34%, yielding orange-colored smoke compositions with high color rendering purity. However, at a GC content of 16 wt %, excessive endothermic cooling caused thermal quenching and interrupted combustion, and FTIR confirmed that the characteristic peaks of the dye were retained in the residue. Overall, a GC content of 8–12 wt % provided the optimal balance between thermal regulation and dye sublimation, offering a quantitative basis for the formulation and design of orange-smoke agents with high colorimetric purity.

item.title: Trivalent-Conjugated-Cation Layered Lead Chloride (Tptz)Pb 2 Cl 7 : Crystal Structure, Electronic Properties, and Photodetection
item.description:
Abstract
Two-dimensional (2D) layered perovskites offer a versatile platform for exploring hybrid halides with tunable optoelectronic properties, owing to their structural diversity and enhanced interlayer coupling. Herein, we report a novel Pb-based 2D layered perovskite (Tptz)Pb2Cl7 (Tptz = 2,4,6-tri(4-pyridyl)-1,3,5-triazine), in which trivalent conjugated Tptz3+ cations are incorporated into this structural family. Single-crystal structure analysis reveals that its structural connectivity resembles the [H3tib]Pb2Br7-type architecture, and DFT calculations further show that strong C–H...Cl hydrogen bonds between the [Pb2Cl7]3– framework and Tptz3+ cations facilitate efficient interlayer carrier transport. More intriguingly, the conjugated cations directly contribute to the band structure, inducing anomalous bandgap narrowing that extends the absorption edge into the visible region, as evidenced by the deep-yellow crystal color. Benefiting from these synergistic effects, the (Tptz)Pb2Cl7 single-crystal photodetector achieves an outstanding on/off ratio of 1.71 × 104, a linear dynamic range (LDR) of 101.83, and a specific detectivity (D*) of 8.02 × 1010 Jones, comparable to those of state-of-the-art Br/I-based perovskite single-crystal devices. Moreover, the device exhibits self-powered photoresponse to X-ray irradiation at 0 V, highlighting its potential for low-power radiation detection.

item.title: Torrefaction-Assisted Fractionation of Material Recovery Facility Waste
item.description:
Abstract
Material recovery facility (MRF) residues are heterogeneous mixtures of plastics, paper/cardboard, and mineral matter that are difficult to separate and are commonly landfilled. This study evaluated whether torrefaction-induced changes in grindability can enable size-based enrichment of plastic-, biogenic-, and mineral-rich components from MRF-derived municipal solid waste (MRF-MSW). Approximately 150 g batches were torrefied at 300–400 °C for 5–150 min, producing 0–55% mass loss, and then ground and vibro-sifted into >850, 74–850, and <74 μm fractions. Across the investigated torrefaction severities, 60–80% of the recovered ash was concentrated in the <74 μm fraction, whereas the >850 μm fraction at low mass loss had the highest higher heating value (HHV) and was enriched in plastics. Microscopy and elemental analysis revealed that the materials were concentrated into plastic, biogenic, and mineral-rich fractions. Above approximately 20% mass loss, all retained material passed the 850 μm screen. The chlorine contribution from the coarse plastic-rich fraction declined to essentially zero above approximately 25% mass loss, while most residual chlorine was associated with the mineral-rich fine fraction. These results show that torrefaction severity can be adjusted to control grindability and facilitate physical fractionation of heterogeneous MRF-MSW.

item.title: Fruit Quality of Tomato Plants Grown under Deficit Irrigation and Treated with Nano-Oxides, Mineral Salts, and Bioinoculants
item.description:
Abstract
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) fruit quality may be affected by deficit irrigation and by Fe, Zn, and microbial inputs. This study evaluated fruit-quality attributes at harvest in HM 2798 tomato under full and deficit irrigation. The experiment was conducted in a 6 × 2 factorial arrangement in a randomized complete block design with four blocks, comprising six treatments and two irrigation regimes, for a total of 48 experimental units. The treatments consisted of a control, ZnO and Fe2O3 nano-oxides, ZnSO4·7H2O and FeSO4·7H2O conventional salts, and a combined commercial bioinoculant treatment (Azokop + No-Nema) applied to the root zone, evaluated under full irrigation (100% crop evapotranspiration, ETc) and deficit irrigation (50% ETc). The Fe and Zn sources were sprayed on the foliage at nonequivalent elemental doses, with the conventional salts supplying approximately five times more Fe or Zn than the nano-oxides. Fruits were harvested once at the USDA Red stage (>90% red surface), and physicochemical attributes, soluble sugars, ascorbic acid, pigments, flavonoids, anthocyanins, and phenolic compounds were evaluated. Under 50% ETc, FeSO4·7H2O resulted in the highest total soluble, reducing, and nonreducing sugar contents, reaching 7.04, 1.23, and 5.81 g 100 g–1 FW, respectively, corresponding to increases of 64.4, 163.2, and 52.3% relative to the control. NPZnO resulted in the highest flavonoid content under 100% ETc (2.47 mg 100 g–1 FW; +27.7% relative to the control). The combined commercial bioinoculant treatment resulted in carotenoid contents of 13.09 and 12.28 mg 100 g–1 FW under 100% and 50% ETc, respectively, with no significant difference between irrigation regimes. ZnSO4·7H2O resulted in the highest phenolic compound content under 100% ETc (32.50 mg GAE 100 g–1 FW; +70.0% relative to the control). Overall, the responses depended on both treatment and irrigation regime, demonstrating specific changes in tomato fruit composition at harvest rather than a uniform mitigation effect of nano-oxides, conventional salts, or bioinoculants. Because dose, formulation, and, for the bioinoculants, application route differed among treatments, these results characterize the specific treatment programs tested rather than the intrinsic efficiency of nano or conventional formulations.

item.title: Preferential Freeze–Thaw Damage in Limestone Containing Stylolites and Calcite Veins from High-Altitude Mining Areas
item.description:
Abstract
Limestone slopes in high-altitude mining areas are subjected to strong diurnal temperature fluctuations and repeated freeze–thaw cycles, which can induce the development of internal pores and cracks and cause structural deterioration of the rock mass. However, where preferential damage occurs and how it affects the structural continuity of limestone remain unclear. To investigate how structural units, including stylolites, calcite veins, and the matrix, control the spatial distribution of freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone, this study examined limestone containing stylolites and calcite veins. The specimens were classified into sparse and dense structural-unit types according to the degree of structural-unit development. Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance T2 spectra, magnetic resonance imaging, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and P-wave velocity tests were combined to reveal the evolution of the pore structure, microscopic damage, and structural continuity under freeze–thaw cycles. The results show that the dense structural-unit specimens exhibited a more pronounced increase in long-T2 components, clustering of high-signal MRI regions, and P-wave velocity attenuation. After 30 freeze–thaw cycles, the velocity attenuation rate of the dense specimens reached 28–30%, significantly higher than that of the sparse specimens, which was 10–12%. The absolute value of the fitted porosity–velocity slope for the dense specimens was approximately 2.17 times that of the sparse specimens. SEM-EDS results indicate that the matrix and calcite vein interiors showed limited changes, although localized crack-like features developed near some vein boundaries after 30 cycles, whereas stylolites gradually evolved into widened, deepened, and rough-bounded banded damage zones, accompanied by relative Ca depletion and local enrichment of Si and Al. These findings demonstrate that freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone is not a uniform accumulation process but a stylolite-dominated preferential damage process controlled by mineralogical-structural heterogeneity. This understanding provides experimental evidence for identifying freeze–thaw damage characteristics and determining key monitoring zones of limestone slopes containing natural structural units in high-altitude mining areas.

item.title: Synthesis of Fused Biimidazole-Containing Polymers and Their Application as High-Potential Organic Cathode Materials for Lithium-Ion Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
The development of sustainable cathode-active materials for lithium-ion batteries requires organic redox systems that combine high reaction potential, sufficient capacity, and cycling stability. High-potential n-type redox-active motifs are particularly attractive because smaller-sized cation insertion generally enables smoother ion diffusion than in p-type systems; however, such materials remain limited. In this study, we report the synthesis of a fused biimidazole-containing polymer, poly(biimidazo[4,5-b]-1,4-benzoquinone) (PBIBQ), and investigate its applicability as a high-potential organic cathode material. PBIBQ was synthesized from tetraamino-1,4-benzoquinone and oxalic acid, and its structure was characterized by solid-state NMR and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Electrochemical measurements revealed that PBIBQ exhibits reversible redox behavior with an average discharge potential of 3.25 V vs Li/Li+ and a specific capacity of 133 mAh g–1, demonstrating one of the highest energy-density levels among nonbenzoquinone/hydroquinone-type organic cathodes. Ex situ XPS analyses and density functional theory calculations support that the biimidazole/tetraazafulvalene-type unit functions as the redox-active center and suggest that Li+ insertion between nitrogen atoms is the dominant charge-storage process. However, PBIBQ suffered a gradual capacity decrease during multicycling due to dissolution of the active material and/or its reduced derivatives. To address this issue, a cross-linked derivative, NW-PBIBQ, was synthesized using a tetrafunctional carboxylic acid linker, and the composite of NW-PBIBQ and multiwalled carbon nanotubes was further prepared to improve charge transport. These approaches successfully suppressed dissolution and lowered charge-transfer resistance, improving rate capability and cycle stability. Overall, these results demonstrate that a fused biimidazole-based polymer is a promising molecular motif to realize high-voltage n-type organic cathode.

item.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Enzymatic Extraction of Flavonoids from Pouteria caimito Leaves: Process Optimization, Mechanistic Investigation, and Bioactivity Evaluation
item.description:
Abstract
To enhance the resource utilization value of Pouteria caimito leaves, this study employed ultrasound-assisted enzymatic extraction (UAE) to extract flavonoids from Pouteria caimito leaves (PCL). The UAE process was optimized using single-factor experiments combined with response surface methodology. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were used to investigate structural changes in leaf tissues and the synergistic extraction effects of ultrasound and enzymatic hydrolysis. UHPLC-HRMS/MS was used to characterize extracts obtained by different extraction methods, and seasonal variations in flavonoid content and biological activity were also evaluated. The optimal extraction conditions were as follows: solid–liquid ratio of 1:50, ethanol concentration of 50%, pH 3.6, enzyme addition of 1.6%, enzymatic hydrolysis temperature of 50 °C, enzymatic hydrolysis time of 51 min, ultrasonic temperature of 50 °C, and ultrasonic time of 39 min. Under these conditions, the flavonoid extraction yield by UAE was higher than that achieved by ultrasonic extraction (UE) or enzymatic extraction (EE) alone. SEM, FT-IR, and XRD results demonstrated more extensive cell wall disruption and higher extraction efficiency with UAE. After purification using AB-8 macroporous resin, flavonoid purity increased from 32.84% to 73.15%. Activity evaluation showed that the purified product (MRP) exhibited strong antioxidant and multienzyme inhibitory activities: DPPH IC50 = (0.0197 ± 0.0014) mg/mL, ABTS+• IC50 = (0.0560 ± 0.0016) mg/mL, tyrosinase IC50 = (0.2911 ± 0.0022) mg/mL, acetylcholinesterase IC50 = (0.5303 ± 0.0101) mg/mL, and α-amylase IC50 = (0.3328 ± 0.0100) mg/mL. Network pharmacology further identified catechin, dihydrotricetin, and kaempferol 3,5,7-trimethyl ether as key candidate compounds and suggested that their potential effects against Alzheimer’s disease may involve AChE-related regulation within the “Neuroactive ligand signaling” pathway. January was identified as the optimal harvest period. This study demonstrates the potential of UAE for the high-value utilization of PCL flavonoids.

item.title: Provenance, Depositional Facies and Favorable Reservoir Distribution of the Lower Cretaceous Yageliemu Formation in the Kuqa Depression, Tarim Basin, NW China
item.description:
Abstract
Tectonic movements and related depositional responses are always complicated in a typical foreland basin. This study investigates the provenance and depositional facies of the Cretaceous Yageliemu Formation in the Kuqa Depression, Tarim Basin, NW China, to determine favorable reservoir distribution. Evidence from detrital zircon U–Pb age and heavy mineral assemblages illustrates two mainly provenances: (1) the Kelasu River characterized by the U–Pb age from 220 to 400 Ma and 420 to 560 Ma and the heavy mineral assemblages of leucoxene, zircon, and barite; (2) the Kuqa River dominated by the U–Pb age from 300 to 520 Ma and the heavy mineral assemblages of barite and apatite. Integration of core, well logging curves, and seismic responses indicates that the Yageliemu Formation can be subdivided into three parasequence sets: EL2, EL1, and LL1. The parasequence sets of EL2 and EL1 are favorable for the development and accumulation of large-scale sand bodies. The sediments in the Yageliemu Formation mainly consist of pebbly sandstone, coarse- to fine-grained sandstone, siltstone, and silty mudstone deposited in a braided-river delta front setting. The braided-river delta front subfacies can be divided into subaqueous distributary channels, proximal mouth bar, and distal mouth bar microfacies. Based on paleogeomorphology reconstruction, seismic attribute facies and core observations, depositional facies and distribution of favorable reservoir facies in the EL1 and EL2 intervals is predicted. This study innovatively identifies two distinct provenance systems, establishes a high-resolution sequence stratigraphic framework, reconstructs the source-to-sink paleogeomorphic configuration, and proposes a hierarchical favorable reservoir prediction model for the Yageliemu Formation. It deepens insights into sedimentary responses of compressional foreland basins and guides ultradeep tight gas exploration in the Kuqa Depression.

item.title: A Previously Unreported Octapeptide from Ganoderma lucidum Attenuates Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in LPS-Stimulated Macrophages via Modulation of NF-κB and COX-2 Signaling
item.description:
Abstract
Ganoderma lucidum is a source of bioactive peptides with reported immunomodulatory properties. In this study, an octapeptide, TNFSNCTL, was identified from G. lucidum hydrolyzates using de novo sequencing coupled with LC–MS/MS and subsequently synthesized via solid-phase peptide synthesis. Querying both the NCBI nonredundant (NR) database and G. lucidum protein sequences returned no exact contiguous alignment, suggesting that TNFSNCTL has not been described before. Its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties were then characterized in cell-free systems and in RAW264.7 macrophages challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Treatment lowered the intracellular levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO) while remaining minimally toxic to fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and macrophages across the concentrations tested. The peptide also downregulated inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and dampened NF-κB p65 phosphorylation, leaving the total NF-κB pool unchanged. As this exploratory study evaluated only low- and high-dose conditions, future studies incorporating intermediate doses will further refine the dose–response relationship and strengthen mechanistic understanding. Proteomic profiling revealed differential regulation of proteins associated with phosphorylation processes, redox homeostasis, and interferon-responsive pathways, including upregulation of Ppp1cc and downregulation of Lrpprc. Molecular docking suggested a potential interaction between TNFSNCTL and COX-2. These findings indicate that TNFSNCTL modulates oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling in macrophages, supporting its potential as a promising candidate for functional food or nutraceutical applications.

item.title: From Mitochondrial Targeting to Microbial Killing: Twinkle-Derived Peptides as an Emerging Class of Potent AMPs
item.description:
Abstract
Mitochondrial targeting sequences are short N-terminal peptides that direct proteins to mitochondria. Notably, their amphipathic α-helical architecture closely resembles that of many potent antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This structural convergence reflects the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and suggests that contemporary mitochondrial targeting sequences may retain latent antimicrobial properties. Here, this evolutionary link was exploited to investigate the mitochondrial-targeting sequences of a Twinkle helicase as a scaffold for the rational design of a new class of antimicrobials. Using an in silico strategy, two peptides, TAMP1 (Twinkle AntiMicrobial Peptide1) and its optimized derivative, TAMP2 (Twinkle AntiMicrobial Peptide2), were designed starting from the mitochondrial targeting sequences of the Twinkle helicase from the Antarctic fish Notothenia coriiceps. Both 18-residue peptides were structurally and functionally characterized as proof of concept for mitochondrial targeting sequence-derived antimicrobials. They adopted stable amphipathic α-helical conformations and exhibited antimicrobial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Notably, TAMP2 demonstrated enhanced efficacy, effectively targeting an extended panel of bacteria, including spoilage, foodborne, and multidrug-resistant pathogens, with MBC values in the range of 0.5–32 μM. Microscale thermophoresis and molecular dynamics simulations further supported these observations, indicating strong interactions with bacterial membrane mimetics and providing mechanistic insight into peptide activity. These findings establish Twinkle-derived mitochondrial targeting sequence peptides as a promising, scalable platform for developing a novel class of antimicrobial agents inspired by mitochondrial evolution.

item.title: Physicochemical Controls on Methane Adsorption Capacity of Coal Seams Beneath Red Beds: Roles of Pore Structure and Surface Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract
The abnormal occurrence of coalbed methane (CBM) beneath thick red beds poses a major challenge to gas disaster prevention and safe coal mining. Previous studies have mainly focused on the sealing capacity of red beds and their influence on CBM migration and accumulation, whereas the response of the underlying coal matrix, particularly its methane adsorption behavior, pore structure, and surface chemistry, remains insufficiently understood. Consequently, the mechanisms linking red beds occurrence conditions to variations in the methane storage capacity of underlying coal seams have not yet been fully quantified. Taking the Xutuan Coal Mine in the Huaibei Coalfield as a case study, this work integrates high-pressure methane adsorption–desorption tests, low-pressure N2/CO2 adsorption experiments, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy to reveal the effects of red beds on methane adsorption behavior, pore structure, and chemical composition of coal. The results show that, with increasing red beds thickness and decreasing distance between the coal seam and the red beds, micropore volume generally decreases, whereas the relative abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups increases. Correlation analysis further shows that methane adsorption capacity is positively correlated with micropore volume and negatively correlated with the relative abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups, with correlation coefficients of 1.0 and −1.0, respectively. These results indicate that both micropore structure and surface chemical characteristics are closely related to the variation in methane adsorption capacity. Combined with the geological characteristics of the red beds, the observed micropore variation may be related to stress-related pore compression, whereas the increase in oxygen-containing functional groups reflects changes in the surface chemical structure of the coal matrix. Fe-related oxidation is proposed as a geochemical hypothesis for the observed variation in oxygen-containing functional groups, based on the regional geological background of the red beds. Furthermore, a normalized red beds geometric influence index, k, was proposed to integrate red beds thickness and its spatial relationship with the coal seam. Field gas content exhibits a strong negative correlation with k, indicating that the proposed index can provide a quantitative reference for the relative evaluation of methane occurrence under comparable red beds geological conditions.

item.title: Multiphase W–V–Hf-Ta Mixed-Metal Oxides for Catalytic Oxidation of Toluene
item.description:
Abstract
Multiphase mixed-metal oxides (MMOs) containing W, V, Hf, Ta, and either Fe or Ti were synthesized by coprecipitation and evaluated as catalysts for toluene oxidation. Structural analysis determined the formation of multiphase crystalline systems, while energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy pointed out to homogeneous elemental distribution. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed that all elements are present in oxidized states, consistent with the formation of mixed-metal oxides. The catalytic activity of the prepared MMO was tested in a fixed-bed reactor in the toluene degradation process. A one-dimensional pseudohomogeneous model assuming first-order kinetics successfully described the experimental data. The Ti-containing catalyst showed slightly higher activity, achieving a lower toluene removal temperature and having a lower activation energy (139.27 kJ mol–1) in comparison to the Fe-containing catalyst (145.41 kJ mol–1). The obtained results demonstrate that the investigated multiphase MMOs are promising candidates for volatile organic compounds removal.

item.title: Tools for Prediction of Alkyne p K a Values: Calculation of Hydrogen Exchange Barriers and NMR Chemical Shifts
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of acidity in terminal alkynes is critical for understanding their chemical behavior in isotope labeling, synthesis design, and drug development. In this study, we evaluate multiple quantum-chemical strategies to identify a reliable and simple computational approach for estimating alkyne acidities. A range of descriptors, including thermodynamic proton and hydrogen atom transfers, reaction energy profiles, vibrational and magnetic properties, and atomic charge distributions, were assessed across a representative set of alkynes. Only two approaches demonstrated predictive performance aligned with experimental data. The first involves calculation of energy barriers for hydrogen exchange, which shows a linear correlation with known pKa values and offers applicability across alkyl-, aryl-, and fluoro-substituted alkynes. The second leverages computed acetylenic proton chemical shifts, which provide valid predictions for a limited subset of alkynes. In contrast, descriptors such as IR frequencies, 13C NMR shifts, and atomic charges failed to yield accurate estimates. We extended our predictions to pharmaceuticals with terminal alkyne groups─such as ethynylestradiol, deprenyl, and 5-ethynyluracil─for which experimental acidity data are currently unavailable. The proposed workflow combines computational efficiency with mechanistic relevance and may serve as a practical tool for chemists seeking to assess the acid–base properties of terminal alkynes in silico.

item.title: Al 3+ -Modified Melamine Sponge for Downhole Oil–Water Separation
item.description:
Abstract
Increasing water production during the later stages of oilfield development generates large volumes of produced water with low oil content, creating challenges for efficient treatment. Downhole oil–water separation can reduce the treatment load of surface facilities but requires materials with high oil selectivity and stable performance. Herein, a hydrophobically modified melamine sponge was prepared through a simple AlCl3 immersion method. SEM-EDS, FTIR, and XPS confirmed the introduction of Al3+ onto the sponge surface and supported its interaction with electron-donating sites in the melamine framework, while the original porous structure was preserved. The modified sponge exhibited water contact angles above 130° and adsorption capacities of approximately 100 g/g for crude oil and 89 g/g for paraffin oil. TGA indicated a modest improvement in thermal stability. Oil–water separation was further evaluated through adsorption, in situ extraction, and filtration. The adsorption mode achieved nearly 100% separation efficiency, while in situ extraction reached 97.5% efficiency at a rate of 6.25 mL/s. Filtration further demonstrated the potential for polishing low-oil-content wastewater. These results highlight Al3+-modified melamine sponge as a simple and versatile material for staged oil–water separation in oilfield applications.

item.title: Simulation of the Deformation Process of a Freely Rising Bubble Using the Lattice Boltzmann Method
item.description:
Abstract
Bubbles exhibit nonlinear motion characteristics in liquids, with their interfaces undergoing significant deformation during movement, resulting in complex and diverse situations. In this paper, the lattice Boltzmann method is employed to numerically simulate the deformation behavior of a freely rising single bubble. The focus is on examining the effects of bubble size, surface tension, liquid viscosity, and liquid density on bubble deformation and obtaining the variation of the Weber number of bubble deformation. The results indicate that the essence of bubble deformation lies in the dynamic interplay between inertial forces, viscous forces, and surface tension. The Weber number serves as an effective comprehensive indicator of the relative importance of these three factors. Notably, surface tension emerges as the pivotal factor inhibiting deformation, whereas liquid density and bubble size facilitate deformation by amplifying inertial forces. The role of liquid viscosity exhibits nonmonotonicity, stemming from its dual function as both a damping dissipator and a shear deformation transmitter.

item.title: A Composable 3D-Printed Platform for Rapid Sequential Sample Injection in Mass Spectrometry
item.description:
Abstract
We developed a composable 3D-printed platform for rapid sequential sample injection in mass spectrometry (MS). The platform works in a well plate-like format and allows direct loading of discrete sample droplets by micropipette or automated liquid handling. Droplets are separated by air gaps during transport and are directly coupled to MS through capillary vibrating sharp-edge spray ionization (cVSSI). Liquid-infused surface treatment was used to improve compatibility of the 3D-printed microchannels with MS analysis. The platform was evaluated for device operation, throughput, quantitative performance, and carryover. A throughput of ∼20 s per sample was achieved at 50 μL/min. Quantitative analysis of lysine gave a linear response with R2 = 0.9986, and carryover was evaluated across chemically distinct small molecules. These results demonstrate that the platform supports air-separated droplet transport, rapid sequential analysis of different samples, and quantitative MS measurements in a simple, modular, and customizable format.
